I have been farming this 5.2 mu plot in Quzhou for 55 years, and my bones know the rhythm of the North China Plain. My wife and I are the only two left in the household, so I keep the plan simple and reliable. The winter wheat I sowed last October is already in the ground; now that it is reviving, I will top-dress it with urea at greening and again at jointing, and irrigate three times through the well—greening water, jointing water, and one more at flowering if the sky stays dry. I will spray herbicide once in early spring and watch for aphids or rust; if they show up, I spray once more. Come early June, I will harvest the wheat, immediately rotary-till the stubble, and plant hybrid maize the same day—timing is everything. For the maize, I will put down compound fertilizer at sowing, then top-dress nitrogen at the big-trumpet stage, irrigate three times depending on the summer rains, and spray for weeds and corn borer. I do not chase fancy seeds; the improved wheat and hybrid maize varieties my neighbors and I have used for years still give me steady yields. I plough before wheat sowing and rotary-till before maize to break the ground without losing too much moisture. At my age, I do not gamble with new tricks—I stick to what has filled our grain jars every year.
